reason: The passage portrays Balak, king of Moab, and his officials unfavorably. Balak is depicted as fearful of the Israelites (וַיָּ֨גָר מוֹאָ֜ב), attempting to manipulate the prophet Balaam through offers of wealth and honor to curse Israel. When Balaam instead blesses Israel, Balak becomes angry (וַיִּֽחַר־ אַ֤ף בָּלָק֙), frustrated that his plans have failed. The narrative emphasizes the elite's powerlessness against God's will—despite being a king with authority, Balak cannot achieve his objectives. His officials are portrayed as mere servants executing his failed commands. The text consistently shows these elite figures as ineffective, self-interested, and ultimately opposed to God's purposes, while contrasting them favorably with blessed Israel.
